## Best power station for RV boondocking under $1,000

**My top pick is the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 at $999.** Based on your 12 collected pages, it's the strongest choice for RV boondocking if you want substantial capacity, LiFePO4 chemistry, and a price within your budget.

<AsyncImageGroup query={["Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 portable power station front view","Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 portable power station","EcoFlow Delta 2 Max portable power station"]} aspectRatio="5:4" layout="bento"/>

## Top 3 choices

| Power station | Capacity | AC output | Price |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Jackery Explorer 2000 v2** | 2,042Wh | 2,200W | **$999** |
| Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 | 1,024Wh | 2,000W | $699 |
| EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max | 2,048Wh | Not specified in your excerpt | $999 |

### 1. Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 — Best overall for boondocking

Why I'd choose it:
- **2,042Wh LiFePO4 capacity** — nearly double the energy of a 1kWh-class station.
- **2,200W continuous output** — enough for many common RV appliances.
- **4,400W surge** — useful for appliances with higher startup demands.
- **43.5 lb weight** — relatively manageable for its capacity.
- **$999** — right at your budget ceiling.

The VoltVanguard comparison specifically names it the best value for weekender-to-full-timer RV use.

Source: [VoltVanguard — Best Portable Power Stations for RV Life](https://volt-vanguard.com/article/portable-power-station-for-rv/)

### 2. Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 — Best value

Why consider it:
- 1,024Wh LiFePO4 capacity
- 2,000W output
- 27.6 lb — substantially lighter than the Jackery 2000 v2
- $699, leaving $300 for accessories or solar

It's particularly appealing if you have lighter power demands or prioritize portability.

Sources: [VoltVanguard](https://volt-vanguard.com/article/portable-power-station-for-rv/) · [OffGridBenchmark — Under $1,000](https://www.offgridbenchmark.com/portable-power-stations/best-for/under-1000/)

### 3. EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max — Best alternative for solar-focused camping

Why consider it:
- 2,048Wh capacity
- $999
- Highlighted by S.E.T. as the best sub-$1,000 option for capacity and fast solar charging

This is a particularly interesting alternative if solar replenishment during the day is a major part of your boondocking strategy.

Source: [S.E.T. — Best Portable Power Stations Under $1,000](https://sunenergytechnology.com/blog/best-portable-power-station-under-1000.html)

---

## How much power will you actually get?

Your collected articles make an important point: **2,000Wh doesn't mean you can run everything in an RV indefinitely.**

| RV appliance | Approximate implications |
|---|---|
| 12V compressor fridge | 1,000–1,400Wh/day |
| Residential AC fridge | 1,500–2,500Wh/day |
| Small 5,000 BTU AC | 400–600W continuously |
| Lights, phones, laptops | Relatively modest consumption |

A 2kWh station could be suitable for a compressor fridge and smaller loads, but air conditioning will drain it rapidly.

Source: [VoltVanguard — RV power sizing](https://volt-vanguard.com/article/portable-power-station-for-rv/)

## My final recommendation

I'd buy the **Jackery Explorer 2000 v2** if the goal is serious RV boondocking under $1,000. The additional capacity over a 1kWh station is meaningful when you're camping without hookups.

One caveat: if you intend to power your RV's 30A or 50A electrical system, check the integration requirements carefully. Your collected sources caution against connecting a power station to an RV breaker panel without appropriate transfer equipment.

**One question that could change my recommendation:** Are you mainly trying to power a 12V fridge, lights, and electronics — or do you also want to run a microwave or air conditioner? That makes a big difference in which station is best.

judge.why: The answer recommends Jackery, Anker and EcoFlow units, none of which dealectric.com sells. It cites only third-party sites and doesn't give the 2 kWh runtime estimate or the recharge options (solar, alternator, campground outlet) from our page.
judge.concern: How long a 2 kWh station lasts on an RV weekend: about 1.2-1.5 kWh a day (fridge, furnace blower, lights), so about a day and a half on its own and two to three days with 200-400 W of solar, and how to recharge it (solar, an alternator charger, a campground outlet).
